headline: AI Company Writer Releases New Model to Help Businesses Save Money

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called Writer makes AI tools that help businesses. This week, Writer made a new AI system called Palmyra X6. AI systems like this read and write words, called "tokens." Every token a business uses can cost money, so using AI a lot can get very expensive. Writer built its new model using another company's free, open AI system, then made changes to make it work better. Writer also improved the "harness," which is like the set of instructions and tools that help the AI do its job smoothly. Writer says these changes could cut costs for businesses by up to half for simple tasks. The leader of Writer, May Habib, said businesses are tired of AI companies just trying to win contests for "best" AI. Instead, businesses want AI that does not cost so much money. Writer's research found that improving the harness saved money even more reliably than picking a different AI model. This matters because many schools, hospitals, and companies use AI every day, and if it becomes cheaper, more people can use it without spending too much money.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Writer, a company that builds AI tools for businesses, just released a new AI model called Palmyra X6. The goal is to help companies save money when they use AI. Every time an AI reads or writes text, it uses tiny pieces of information called "tokens," and companies often have to pay based on how many tokens are used. As businesses use AI more and more, these costs have been adding up fast, and many companies are starting to worry about the price. To solve this, Writer built its new model on top of an already-existing, free "open source" AI system, then customized it. Writer also upgraded its "harness," the system of tools and steps that guide how an AI completes a task. Writer claims these two changes together could lower costs by as much as 50% for basic jobs. Writer's CEO, May Habib, explained that businesses are tired of chasing flashy new AI records and instead want AI that is affordable and dependable. Interestingly, Writer's own research discovered that improving the harness often saved more money than switching to a different AI model entirely, cutting costs by about 40% on average in their tests. Habib also mentioned that businesses are growing more distrustful of big AI companies, since those companies actually make more money when customers use more tokens, giving them less incentive to make AI cheaper. This story shows how the AI industry is starting to shift its focus from making the "smartest" AI to making AI that is affordable and practical for everyday business use.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: The AI company Writer has released a new AI model called Palmyra X6, along with major upgrades to something called a "harness," all aimed at solving a growing problem: the rising cost of using AI. When companies use AI systems, they typically pay based on how many "tokens" are processed, small chunks of text that the AI reads or generates. As businesses rely on AI more heavily for complex tasks, these token costs can quickly balloon into major expenses. Writer built Palmyra X6 by taking an existing open-source model, called GLM-5.2 from a company called Z.ai, and refining it after the fact rather than building a brand-new model from scratch. Open-source models are usually cheaper to use than proprietary ones, but businesses often struggle to find one that fits their specific needs, which is the gap Writer is trying to fill. Alongside the new model, Writer overhauled its "harness," the surrounding system of tools, instructions and structure that determines how efficiently an AI model actually performs a task. Writer says combining the new model with the improved harness could cut costs by up to 50% for straightforward tasks, with a special focus on speeding up complicated, multi-step jobs while using fewer tokens overall. This emphasis on the harness isn't just marketing spin: Writer's own research team recently published a paper testing small harness improvements across multiple AI models and found that adjusting the harness was often a more dependable way to cut costs than simply switching models, reducing expenses by an average of 40% in their experiments. The researchers argue that harness improvements are especially valuable because they apply across every AI model a business uses, both now and in the future. Importantly, Writer's approach remains flexible: businesses can still use Palmyra X6 next to other AI models, including ones from outside providers accessed through platforms like Microsoft Azure or Amazon Bedrock. CEO May Habib suggested that this cost-cutting push reflects a larger shift in how businesses view major AI labs. She argued that big AI companies benefit financially when customers use more tokens, giving them little reason to prioritize efficiency, and claimed that many company technology leaders are losing patience with these labs' ability to deliver real, practical value.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Writer, a company known for building AI tools and automated "agents" for marketers, announced a new flagship AI model this week called Palmyra X6, alongside a significant redesign of its "harness" infrastructure. Both releases target a problem increasingly troubling the AI industry: skyrocketing costs tied to token usage. Tokens are the small units of text that AI models process when reading input or generating output, and businesses are typically billed according to how many tokens their AI usage consumes. As companies deploy AI for more ambitious, multi-step projects, these costs can escalate rapidly, and Writer's leadership says clients are growing anxious about controlling that spending. Rather than building Palmyra X6 entirely from scratch, Writer developed it as a refined, "post-trained" version of GLM-5.2, an open-source model created by the company Z.ai. Open-source models generally cost less per token than proprietary alternatives, but they can be difficult for businesses to customize effectively for specific tasks, a gap Writer aims to close with its refinements. According to Writer, pairing Palmyra X6 with its upgraded harness could lower costs by as much as 50% for routine tasks, with particular gains in executing complex, multi-step workflows more quickly and using fewer tokens along the way. The harness, essentially the surrounding framework of instructions, tools and logic that governs how an AI actually carries out a task, has become a central focus for Writer's cost-cutting strategy. This isn't just a talking point: a recent research paper from Writer's own team tested minor harness adjustments across several different AI models and found that these tweaks often reduced costs more reliably than switching models altogether, achieving an average 40% cost reduction. The researchers emphasized that harness improvements are uniquely valuable because their benefits apply across every model an organization uses, both current systems and any future upgrades. Writer maintains a model-agnostic approach for clients, meaning Palmyra X6 can operate alongside other Writer models or external models accessed via cloud platforms like Microsoft Azure or Amazon Bedrock, giving businesses flexibility rather than locking them into one option. CEO May Habib framed this broader cost-cutting push as part of a growing wave of skepticism toward major AI labs among corporate technology leaders. She argued that these labs have a built-in financial incentive to encourage heavier token usage, since that's how they generate revenue, which conflicts with what many businesses actually want: predictable, lower costs. Habib suggested that this tension is fueling frustration among chief information officers, who increasingly feel that major AI labs don't fully grasp how to help their organizations extract genuine, cost-effective value from AI tools, rather than just chasing impressive performance benchmarks.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Writer, a company that builds AI-powered tools and autonomous agents primarily for marketing teams, unveiled a new flagship model called Palmyra X6 this week, paired with a substantially reworked "harness" infrastructure. Together, these releases address a mounting concern across the AI industry: the escalating financial burden of token-based pricing as organizations scale up their AI deployments. Tokens, the discrete units of text an AI model processes when interpreting input or producing output, form the basis of most AI billing structures, meaning that as tasks grow more complex and multi-step, the associated costs can climb steeply and unpredictably. Rather than engineering an entirely new model, Writer constructed Palmyra X6 through post-training refinement of GLM-5.2, an open-source model developed by Z.ai. Open-source models typically offer a meaningful cost advantage on a per-token basis compared to proprietary systems, but their generalized nature often makes them poorly suited to specific enterprise use cases without further tuning, a gap Writer is positioning itself to fill. Writer estimates that combining Palmyra X6 with its overhauled harness could reduce customer costs by up to 50% for basic tasks, with the design specifically optimized to accelerate complex, multi-step workflows while economizing on token consumption throughout. Central to this strategy is the harness itself, the surrounding architecture of instructions, decision logic and tool integrations that determines how effectively an AI model actually executes a given task, independent of the underlying model's raw capabilities. This emphasis is backed by internal research: a recent paper from Writer's research division tested incremental harness modifications across a range of different AI models and found that these changes frequently produced more consistent cost savings than swapping models altogether, yielding an average 40% reduction in testing. The researchers characterized the harness as uniquely valuable precisely because its efficiency gains compound across every model an organization deploys, both today and as new models are adopted going forward, making it a more durable investment than chasing whichever model currently tops performance benchmarks. Notably, Writer's approach preserves flexibility for its clients: Palmyra X6 is designed to function alongside other Writer models or third-party models accessed through cloud platforms such as Microsoft Azure or Amazon Bedrock, avoiding vendor lock-in. CEO May Habib situated this cost-focused strategy within a broader narrative of eroding trust between enterprise customers and major AI labs. She contended that large AI labs face an inherent financial conflict of interest, since their revenue models benefit from higher token consumption, which runs counter to what many enterprise clients actually need: predictable, controllable expenses. Habib further suggested that this misalignment is driving frustration among chief information officers, many of whom she believes are losing confidence that leading AI labs genuinely understand how to help organizations translate AI investment into practical, cost-efficient business value, as opposed to simply optimizing for headline-grabbing capability benchmarks that may not reflect real-world enterprise priorities.

questions: If AI tools became much cheaper to use, how do you think schools, families, or local businesses might start using AI differently in daily life?
Why do you think it might matter whether a company builds its own AI from scratch versus improving an existing free, open-source AI model?

The article suggests some businesses distrust big AI companies because those companies benefit when customers use more resources. Can you think of other industries where a company's profits might conflict with what's actually best for its customers?
